# Efficiency and High Performance Computing

# Efficiency

## Loops

Example: Square Roots
```{r}

# Using a for loop
forLoopRoots <- function(n){
  roots <- rep(NA, n)
  for(i in 1:n){
    roots[i] <- sqrt(i)
  }
  return(roots)
}

head(forLoopRoots(10000))

# Using sapply
SapplyRoots <- function(n){
  roots <- sapply(1:n, sqrt)
  return(roots)
}

head(SapplyRoots(10000))

library(microbenchmark)
microbenchmark(forLoopRoots(10000), SapplyRoots(10000))

# Using vectorization to perform all calculations "at once"
VectorizedRoots <- function(n){
  sqrt(1:n)
}

head(VectorizedRoots(10000))
microbenchmark(forLoopRoots(10000), VectorizedRoots(10000))

# Anytime you can use vectorized computation, you should
```

## Pre-made functions

Aim to write as little code as possible

Example: Repeated Elements
```{r}
set.seed(1)
vec <- sample(letters, 100, replace = TRUE)
vec

# Using two nested loops
method1 <- function(x){
  # first element cannot be a duplicate
  out <- sapply(2:length(x), function(i){
    matches <- sapply(1:(i-1), function(i2){
      x[i2] == x[i]
    })
    return(any(matches))
  })
  out <- c(FALSE, out)
  return(out)
}

vec[1:11]

method1(vec)[1:11]

# Loop and Vectorized Comparison
method2 <- function(x){
  # first element cannot be a duplicate
  out <- sapply(2:length(x), function(i){
    return(any(x[1:(i-1)] == x[i]))
  })
  out <- c(FALSE, out)
  return(out)
}

method2(vec)[1:11]
microbenchmark(method1(vec), method2(vec))

# Base function: duplicated
method3 <- function(x){
  duplicated(x)
}

method3(vec)[1:11]
microbenchmark(method2(vec), method3(vec))

# Check to see if the methods all give the same output. If not, then the methods are not the same. Use this to check your optimized method.

method2(vec) == method3(vec)
method1(vec) == method2(vec)
method1(vec) == method3(vec)
```

# High Performance Computing

HPC can be:
Parallel Computing - using multiple resources simultaneously to complete a task
Big data working with large datasets

Parallelization - take full advantage of computer by using all cores at the same time. Will reduced computation time.

A function is parallelizable if each individual item does not depend on other elements. 


Parallelization Packages: parallel, foreach, and future. Implicit parrelism are out-of-the-box tools that allow the programmer not to worry about parallelization. Because R is built in C, the packages Rcpp and OpenMP are also good. 

The parallel package: explicit parallelism, parallel computing as multiple R sessions
1. Create a PSOCK/FORK cluster using makePSOCKCluster/makeForkCluster
2. Copy/prepare each R session (if using PSOCK cluster): copy objects with clusterExport, set a seed with clusterSetRNGStream
3. Do your call: Pass expressions with clusterEvalQ, Run a parallelized loop with parApply, parLappy, etc.
4. Stop the cluster with stopCluster

## Example: Hello World!
```{r}
# 1. CREATING A CLUSTER
library(parallel)
cl <- makeCluster(4)    
x  <- 20

# 2. PREPARING THE CLUSTER
clusterSetRNGStream(cl, 123) # Equivalent to `set.seed(123)` (not necessary for this example)
clusterExport(cl, "x")

# 3. DO YOUR CALL
clusterEvalQ(cl, {
  paste0("Hello from process #", Sys.getpid(), ". I see x and it is equal to ", x)
})

# 4. STOP THE CLUSTER
stopCluster(cl)

# Multi-core version of apply functions
# 1. SETUP
library(parallel)
x  <- 20

# 2. DO YOUR CALL
mclapply(1:4, function(i){
    paste0("Hello from process #", Sys.getpid(), ". I see x and it is equal to ", x)
}, mc.cores = 4)
```

## Parallel Regression

Run multiple regressions on a wide dataset 
y=Xiβi+ε,ε∼N(0,σ2i),∀i

```{r}
# Serial Solution, use apply to solve it
library(parallel)
cl <- makeCluster(4L)
clusterExport(cl, "y")
ans <- parApply(
  cl = cl,
  X = X,
  MARGIN = 2,
  FUN = function(x) coef(lm(y ~ x))
)
 
ans[,1:5]

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  parallel = parApply(
    cl = cl,
    X = X, MARGIN = 2,
    FUN = function(x) coef(lm(y ~ x))
  ),
  serial = apply(
    X = X, MARGIN = 2,
    FUN = function(x) coef(lm(y ~ x))
  ), unit="relative"
)
```

# Extended Example: SARS-CoV2 Simulation (an altered version of Conway's Game of Life)

1. People live on a grid, each individual has 8 neighbors
2. A helathy individual (A) interacting with a sick neighbor (B) has the probabilities: 100% if none wear a mask, 50% if A wears a mask, 20% if B wears a mask, and 5% if both wear a mask
3. Infected individuals may die with probability 10%

We are going to simulate a system with 2,500 (50 x 50) individuals, 1,000 times so we can analyze: (a) contagion curve, (b) death curve.

```{r}
# source("~/Downloads/sars-cov2.R", echo=FALSE)
source("img/sars-cov2.R", echo = FALSE)

# Looking at some constants
probs_sick # Sick individual's probabilities

set.seed(7123)
one <- simulate_covid(
    pop_size = 1600,
    nsick = 160,
    nwears_mask = 1:400,
    nsteps = 20,
    store = TRUE
)

one$statistics[c(1:5, 16:20),]

# Location of who wears the facemask. This step is only for plotting
wears <- which(one$wears, arr.ind = TRUE) - 1
wears <- wears/(one$nr) * (1 + 1/one$nr)

# Initializing the animation
fig   <- magick::image_device(600, 600, res = 96/2, pointsize = 24)
for (i in 1:one$current_step) {
  
  # Plot
  image(
    one$temporal[,,i], col=c("gray", "tomato", "steelblue","black"),
    main = paste("Time", i - 1L, "of", one$nsteps),
    zlim = c(1,4)
    )
  points(wears, col="white", pch=20, cex=1.5)
  legend(
    "topright",
    col = c("gray", "tomato", "steelblue","black", "black"),
    legend = c(names(codes), "wears a mask"),
    pch = c(rep(15, 4), 21)
  )
}

# Finalizing plot and writing the animation
dev.off()
animation <- magick::image_animate(fig, fps = 2)
magick::image_write(animation, "covid1.gif")
```
